newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan changes law to lift ban on holding companies.
newsitem.headline: Japan changes law to lift ban on holding companies.

text.p: Japan changed its anti-monopoly law on Wednesday to lift a ban on holding companies that was imposed by U.S. Occupation forces after World War Two.
Parliament's Upper House passed a revised law which will allow firms to set up holding companies as long as doing so would not cause an excessive concentration of business strength.
Japan's anti-monopoly watchdog said the revision will take effect by December 18, although an exact date during that six-month period has not been determined.

The revised law clears the way for telecommunications giant Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT) to realise its long-held dream of entering the global market, through a restructuring which will split it into two regional local carriers and one long-distance group under a holding company.
Financial firms, however, are still not allowed to set up holding companies until related financial laws are revised.
U.S. Occupation forces introduced the ban on holding companies in 1947 to break up powerful conglomerates known as "zaibatsu" which the United States believed had contributed to Japan's war effort.
Holding companies are firms which control one or more other firms, often by holding a majority stake in them, but do not themselves engage in a specific business.
An official at Japan's anti-monopoly watchdog, the Fair Trade Commission (FTC), said it may take some time to lift the remaining barriers to financial firms setting up holding companies.
"Legal procedures to allow banks to set up holding companies have been delayed and it is unlikely that revisions to the related financial laws will take effect by the end of 1997," the official said.
Industry sources said that the Finance Ministry was expected to allow banks to set up financial holding firms sometime in the next fiscal year, starting on April 1, 1998.
Big business and financial institutions have called for the ban to be lifted to help them streamline and compete with overseas rivals.
To prevent an excessive concentration of business strength, the anti-monopoly watchdog will work out detailed guidelines before the revised law takes effect, the FTC official said.
The watchdog has already stated the three types of holding companies which would be regarded as preventing fair and free competition among companies.

These are extremely large corporate groups whose total assets exceed about 15 trillion yen ($135 billion), corporate groups headed by a large financial institution and groups formed by major companies in the same or related industries.
The revised law will also require corporations with total assets of up to 300 billion yen ($2.70 billion) which want to set up holding companies to notify the FTC in advance, the official said.
